_comment: Shipped defaults. Resolution order, later wins, shallow-merged per top-level key: (1) this file, (2) ~/.config/claude-qa-manager/config.json (user-level: credentials, policy), (3) <repo>/.claude/skills/qa-cycle/config.json (project-level: targets, schema files). A project should never need to restate credentials, and a user config should never need to know a repo's layout.

targets._comment: Optional. Branches are derived at runtime from the MR/PR itself, so single-repo projects need NO targets at all. Declare targets only for a monorepo whose submodules are reviewed independently. See examples/monorepo-submodules.json.

schema._comment: Paths that ARE the database schema -- the file(s) a provisioner reads to create a new tenant/instance. Empty by default: when empty the schema gate reports 'skipped:not-configured' and NEVER silently passes. Match on path only; do NOT add DDL content scanning (see docs/CASE-STUDIES.md #schema-drift).

contract._comment: How a ticket id is recognised in an MR/PR title or body.

qa_agent._comment: Optional separate identity for QA-attributed actions (round notes, approvals). Fix commits and pushes always use the developer's own credentials. When unresolvable, the plugin degrades gracefully: notes post under the dev identity and approval is skipped entirely.

progress._comment: How long the lens fan-out may go quiet before a renderer calls it stalled. The status file is rewritten when a lens RETURNS, so the legitimate silence between writes is however long your slowest lens takes -- which is a property of YOUR repo and diff, not of this tool. A 595-line diff on a large monorepo ran 8-20 minutes per lens; a small service may finish in seconds, and there a 20-minute fuse means a genuinely wedged round goes unnoticed for 20 minutes. Tune it down for a fast project, up for a slow one. Only the fan-out needs this: the manager's own merge/render/post phases are bounded work and use a short fixed threshold. QA_STATUS_LENS_STALL_SECONDS overrides it without touching config.

verify._comment: How a fix is verified before it is committed. Normally EMPTY: the target's own test/build entry point is DISCOVERED from its Makefile, package.json, tox.ini, go.mod, etc. Any decent project already declares how it is tested, and restating that here duplicates it -- the copy then drifts and the gate certifies a command the project stopped using. An override must name ANOTHER ENTRY POINT THE PROJECT ALREADY PROVIDES -- never a subset of a detected recipe. A test target is an interface; its recipe is the implementation, and that implementation routinely encapsulates things invisible from outside: bringing up a container, placing fixture files, clearing volumes, waiting for a database. Lift the inner command out of it and you keep the appearance of a test run while discarding everything the target existed to guarantee, and a partial invocation still exits zero, so the loss is silent. If the discovered command has side effects you cannot accept, name the project's other entry point (a container-scoped target, a narrower suite target); do not synthesise a third command from the first one's insides. Set `command` only when detection is wrong, and prefer the PER-TARGET form `targets.<name>.verify.command`, which wins over this one: in a monorepo the parts differ, and one submodule's detected `npm test` can be correct while a sibling's detected `make test` also tears the dev environment down. Detection finds A test entry point, not necessarily a SAFE one -- it checks that a target exists, not what its recipe does. When nothing is discoverable the gate reports state 'none-found' and the round note must say the fixes went unverified; it NEVER reports a pass.
verify._comment_expect: A regex (ERE) that MUST appear in the run's output for the round to call it a pass. EXIT 0 IS NOT A PASS: a test entry point that starts services, runs a harness and tears them down again reports the status of the LAST thing it did, which is the teardown -- so a harness that aborted before running anything still exits 0. Name the string YOUR harness prints when it genuinely succeeds ('All tests successful', 'Result: PASS', '0 failures'). Nothing here knows any harness's output format and nothing should be added that does; the configured regex is the only string this tool ever matches. Leave it EMPTY and the state is 'unconfirmed', never 'passed': the command exited cleanly but nothing establishes that a suite ran, which is the same class of report as 'none-found'. Only a CONFIRMED pass feeds the learned baseline -- timing a run that tested nothing teaches the bound nonsense. Per-target form `targets.<name>.verify.expect` wins over this one. /qa-init can propose a value by reading the project's own documented test procedure.
verify._comment_timeout: Seconds the fix step may let the verify command run before it is killed (TERM, then KILL, on the whole process group). Detection proves a test entry point EXISTS; it never proves the command TERMINATES, and nothing between detection and execution establishes that it is autonomous -- a `scripts.test` that resolves to a watcher, or any suite that reads stdin, blocks the round with nothing to kill it. A killed run reports state 'timeout', which is NOT a pass: like 'none-found' it means the round has no execution evidence. Per-target form `targets.<name>.verify.timeout_seconds` wins over this one. Raise it for a legitimately slow suite; do not raise it to accommodate a watcher -- name the project's non-watch entry point in `verify.command` instead.
verify._comment_baseline: The flat ceiling above is safe but blunt: a 20-second suite that wedges still burns the whole allowance before anyone looks. So the bound is also LEARNED from how long this target's own verify command has actually taken. Only the declared `verify.command` is measured -- a round runs other things through the same helper (a red-first check on one test file is seconds where the suite is minutes) and pooling them would let the narrow run set the bound for the suite. Only runs that TERMINATED are recorded; recording a timeout would ratchet the bound upward using the number that means 'this did not finish'. Durations live OUTSIDE the repo, under ~/.config/claude-qa-manager/verify-timings/, because they are observed local data, not configuration -- one machine's timings are wrong for everyone else's hardware. Every value here is policy, not a law: they were first chosen against one project's suite, and a generic driver must not carry one project's calibration. `min_samples: 0` disables the learned bound and leaves the flat ceiling. Per-target form `targets.<name>.verify.baseline` wins over this one.

review._comment: Panel width is capped at 6 -- the measured concurrency ceiling for agent grandchildren, which keeps the panel a single wave. Narrow a target's lens_tags rather than overriding the panel by hand, and never manage cost by downgrading the model: a cheaper reviewer is a weaker reviewer, which defeats the cycle. Every lens runs on an explicitly named model, never the session's: a lens that inherited would review on Haiku whenever the operator's session runs Haiku. `model` names it for the whole panel, `lens_models` per lens (keys are LENS NAMES like 'contract-security', not lens_tags like 'api' -- lens_models wins over `model` for a lens it names). `allowed_models` is the floor, an enumerated allow-list and never a strength ranking: every resolved model must contain one entry (case-insensitive substring, so 'opus' admits 'claude-opus-5' and 'opus[1m]'), or preflight refuses the round with exit 2 -- an empty `model` included. run-panel.sh checks the same list against the model each lens ACTUALLY ran as (its modelUsage), and a lens that ran below it is recorded as failed with its findings discarded. Widen the list deliberately, not to make a round start.
review._test_path_comment: Which paths are TEST scaffolding rather than code a customer executes. Empty means the built-in default in lib/attribute-findings.sh, which covers tests?/ specs?/ __tests__/ testing/ dirs, *.test.* / *.spec.* / *_test.*, a bare test.<ext>, and Perl .t -- matched case-insensitively. It exists because a MINOR finding on the cycle's own fix is routed by it: in a test file it goes to the observations ledger, in production code it is still offered as a fix. Measured over a month, 60 of 200 self-inflicted findings were minor defects in test scaffolding the fix round itself wrote. Set this only if your tests live somewhere the default misses; it REPLACES the default rather than adding to it, so include the ordinary cases too. Path matching only -- never file content, for the reason docs/CASE-STUDIES.md §schema-drift records.

sast_gate._comment: Behaviour when a security pipeline is still running on an approval-eligible round. Poll cadence is deliberately coarse to stay friendly to prompt caching.
